rows.name: bash
rows.blurb: A target-only shell language. Generate scripts with correct quoting: a lifted Rust string becomes a double-quoted word with `"`, `\`, `$` and backticks escaped, so the value stays inert data.

cells.note: derived from the grammar's `REPEAT` rules by `bin/gen-arity`; agrees with zsh's table on every shared node kind except `function_definition`, where the two grammars themselves differ
no `typ()` override, so every tag reports the default `File`
strings and integers only — the shells are word-oriented, so there is no float or bool `LiftTo<Bash>` impl
target-only: no `MetaLanguage`, so the host's meta drives expansion
target-only: nothing to lift from
target-only: no meta-language to reduce with
target-only: `←` is the *host's* operator, so this language has no emit of its own. What matters for a target is having variadic containers to receive emitted children, which is the Variadic axis
target-only; bash fragments can still be destructured by a Rust host
`hashbang()` returns `#!/usr/bin/env bash`, but bash has no `MetaLanguage` so it can never be a ground language — the shebang is unreachable through `quilt run`
target-only: no runtime library

detail: bare `↖…↗` in a chain resolves to bash

cells.note: target-only: never the ground language, so no generated-file header is produced
embedded-quote highlighting only, from the vendored `highlights.scm`; no downstream bash server is proxied

rows.name: html
rows.blurb: A target-only language for code-generated pages, reports and templates. The Python and TypeScript hosts lift values into it through `qlift_html`, which entity-escapes so a lifted value is inert as text or as an attribute value.

cells.note: holes work in text, in node position and inside double-quoted attribute values; in an attribute value a hole must not follow literal text, because the value's maximal token swallows the marker
no `typ()` override, so every tag reports the default `File`
no `LiftTo<Html>` marker, so a Rust host cannot lift into an HTML quote; the Python and TypeScript hosts lift through `qlift_html` instead, which is a host-side spelling rather than a `LiftTo` impl
target-only: no `MetaLanguage`, so the host's meta drives expansion
target-only: nothing to lift from
target-only: no meta-language to reduce with
target-only: `←` is the *host's* operator, so this language has no emit of its own. What matters for a target is having variadic containers to receive emitted children, which is the Variadic axis
target-only; HTML fragments can still be destructured by a Rust host
a document is rendered by a browser, not executed
target-only: no runtime library
`report.html.py.quilt` makes bare quotes default to HTML inside a Python host
detail: bare `↖…↗` in a chain resolves to html

cells.note: target-only: never the ground language, so no generated-file header is produced
embedded-quote highlighting only, from the vendored `highlights.scm`; no downstream HTML server is proxied

rows.name: lean
rows.blurb: A quotable target and a string-based host. Generate definitions, theorems and tactic proofs at build time; as a host, a `.lean.quilt` metaprogram expands to plain Lean that builds the output with `s!"…"` interpolation.

cells.note: term, tactic, do-element, declaration-name and binder position all work with the unpatched grammar (`__QUILT_HOLE__` matches Lean's identifier regex); whole-command position is reached only by the `#check …` wrapper fallback in `parse_pre`
no reduce backend: the string-based meta has no `QTerm` runtime to evaluate against

`emit_str` fails unconditionally: the string-based meta has no `b_` accumulator for `←` to append to, and the error points at `List.map` + `String.intercalate` instead. Automatic emission of children into the variadic `by` / `do` containers is a separate mechanism (`wrap_child`) and is unaffected; a top-level sequence of commands additionally needs a variadic `module`
no `pattern_tag`/`pattern_var` implementation; Lean fragments can still be destructured by a Rust host
Lean has no interpreter shebang — a file runs via `lean file.lean` or `lake env lean`, and `#!` is not Lean comment syntax
string-based meta: no `QTerm` runtime library is shipped for Lean

`←` is Lean's monadic bind and is eaten by the emit glyph; `↑` (coercion) and `↓` (lowering) are also real Lean notation. The ASCII alias `<-` is the current workaround, and `\←` does not escape because `←` is missing from the grammar's escape class

detail: bare `↖…↗` in a chain resolves to lean

cells.note: generated Lean files use `--`, not `//!`
Lean is a host with a `MetaLanguageAdapter` since #135

rows.name: nix
rows.blurb: A quotable target and a string-based host. Generate derivations, flakes and modules at build time; as a host, a `.nix.quilt` metaprogram expands to plain Nix that builds the output with `${…}` antiquotation.

cells.note: Nix is purely expression-oriented, so every position is an expression and `__QUILT_HOLE__` parses unpatched as a `variable_expression`
no reduce backend: the string-based meta has no `QTerm` runtime to evaluate against

the string model has no `b_` accumulator, so `←` is the *functional* reading of emit: it takes the whole list of fragments and joins it into the surrounding container (`builtins.concatStringsSep "\n"`, applied prefix like `↑`). Building that list is `map`, not a ground loop, and joined fragments are not re-indented
no `pattern_tag`/`pattern_var` implementation; Nix fragments can still be destructured by a Rust host
a `.nix` file is evaluated with `nix eval`, not executed, so there is no shebang runner
string-based meta: no `QTerm` runtime library is shipped for Nix

detail: bare `↖…↗` in a chain resolves to nix

cells.note: generated Nix files use `#`, not `//!`
embedded-quote highlighting only, from the vendored `highlights.scm`; no downstream Nix server is proxied

rows.name: python
rows.blurb: The second host. The PyO3 module in `quilt-python/` gives Python the same `QTerm` builder API the Rust runtime has, and `PythonMetaLanguage` expands quotes into calls against it.

cells.note: no statement-splice: the fluent `.e(child)` chain has no named `b_` accumulator the way the Rust variadic block does, so emit from a ground loop is unavailable

`PythonMetaLanguage` sets no `pattern_tag`, so a Python host cannot write `let ↖…↗ = …`. Python *fragments* can still be destructured by a Rust host, which is what `expand_rust.rs::pattern_let_runtime` exercises

detail: bare `↖…↗` in a chain resolves to python

rows.name: rust
rows.blurb: The primary host. Its `MetaLanguage` is generated from `mk_meta.rs.quilt` by the two-stage bootstrap, so the expander that produces Rust is itself written in Quilt.

cells.note: the LSP projects Rust to rust-analyzer rather than highlighting it from a vendored query

detail: bare `↖…↗` in a chain resolves to rust

rows.name: text
rows.blurb: Quote an arbitrary fragment with no language-specific parsing — useful for generating configuration, prose or any format Quilt has no grammar for. A text term is one `text` tuple whose commands interleave literal runs with holes.

detail: multiline → Tuple text ⟨"line one", ⏎, "line two", ⏎, ⏎, "line four"⟩
glyph_like_content → Tuple text ⟨"arrows and braces: {} ${} <- stay literal"⟩

cells.note: text imposes no kind on a hole, so a spliced child is rendered however the host built it
a text fragment is always an opaque value, so `typ()` answers `Expr` for every tag
no `LiftTo<Text>` marker; a host that wants a value as text lifts it in its own language and splices the result
plain text has no grammar to highlight
the `TextMetaLanguage` exists but is identity-only and is not registered as a host in `Omni`
not a host: nothing to lift from
not a host: no meta-language to reduce with
target-only: `←` is the *host's* operator, so this language has no emit of its own. What matters for a target is having variadic containers to receive emitted children, which is the Variadic axis
target-only; text fragments can still be destructured by a Rust host
plain text is not executable
target-only: no runtime library

detail: bare `↖…↗` in a chain resolves to text

cells.note: target-only: never the ground language, so no generated-file header is produced
nothing to project: plain text has no downstream server

rows.name: typescript
rows.blurb: The host behind the browser playground. Expanded `.ts.quilt` code calls the `quilt-wasm` runtime, so a metaprogram can run in the browser with no server — or under node, where `quilt run` binds the same runtime and adds `↓`.

cells.note: no `LiftTo<TypeScript>` marker in `lift.rs`, so a Rust host cannot lift a value into a TypeScript quote; the TypeScript host lifts its own values through the wasm runtime's `qlift`
no `highlights.scm` is vendored for the TypeScript grammar
`quilt run` binds the bare `quilt` import to the Node runtime (`quilt-wasm/node`), which re-expands a generated stage by shelling out to the `quilt` binary; needs `bin/build-ts`
same fluent-chain shape as Python: no named accumulator, so emit from a ground loop is unavailable
no `pattern_tag`/`pattern_var` implementation; pattern lets are a Rust-host feature

detail: bare `↖…↗` in a chain resolves to typescript

cells.note: no `LanguageAdapter`; `.ts.quilt` files get no projection

rows.name: wgsl
rows.blurb: WebGPU Shading Language — a target-only language. Generate shader code at build time from a Rust or Python host, lifting host values straight into WGSL literal syntax.

cells.note: no `typ()` override, so every tag reports the default `File`; WGSL instead sorts fragments with `classify_term`, which reads the parsed term rather than the tag

numeric and bool literals only — WGSL has no string type, so no `LiftTo<Wgsl> for str` impl exists and lifting a string is a compile error in the generated program rather than a silent truncation. 64-bit integers are likewise omitted
the LSP vendors a patched WGSL highlight query of its own rather than exposing one from `quilt::grammars`
target-only: no `MetaLanguage`, so the host's meta drives expansion
target-only: nothing to lift from
target-only: no meta-language to reduce with

target-only; WGSL fragments can still be destructured by a Rust host
a shader is compiled by the host application, not executed directly
target-only: no runtime library
the canonical chain case: `shaders.wgsl.rs.quilt` makes bare quotes default to WGSL
detail: bare `↖…↗` in a chain resolves to wgsl
